body:
The objection slot arrived empty ("absent in the first template invocation"), so the only criticisms actually on the table are the account's own o1 and the rival's r9. I will not reconstruct a missing one. What I have is an account, a rival, and the question of what to do with both.

The two readings are not rivals in the strict sense. The account says the friction is mostly specification ambiguity under shifting schedules; the rival says the disputes may be about what kind of household this is, and that writing specifications down enacts one side of that question. The rival concedes it may be a second axis rather than a replacement, and the account's closing test — if tightened specs don't stop recurrence, the problem is relational — already concedes the rival's case as its own failure condition. So I am not choosing between them. I am choosing an order of operations that produces evidence for both at low cost and minimal added pressure on the person already leaving the room.

What converges, and is therefore most robust: both accounts end at the same terminal move. If engagement keeps failing, stop optimizing chores and name the question of whether the living arrangement fits (account's step 5, rival's r11). Two different diagnoses landing on the same endpoint makes that the strongest item on the table; it stays, unchanged, as the named last resort rather than something drifted into.

From the account I keep: small concrete recurring items instead of a general fairness summit (c2, u1), and the one-to-one narrow ask to the avoiding friend (c3). From the rival I keep: r7, the most useful single instrument offered by either side — when a specification is proposed, watch whether the withdrawing flatmate engages with its content or pulls back from the proposal itself — and r10's caution not to aggregate separate conversations into a group settlement.

The merged first move, which revises both: pick two or three genuinely recurring items, write the account's three columns for each (done, by when, fallback), and propose the draft to each flatmate separately as something they can mark up — not as a shared note unveiled to the group. This revises the account's step 2 in delivery only: same test, individual rather than group presentation. Grounds: the rival's r3 caution, the account's own c3 logic, and cheapness — one ten-minute conversation per person simultaneously runs u1's recurrence test and r7's form/content observation. If both engage with content, consolidate the shared note and proceed on the account's path. If the withdrawing flatmate pulls back from the form — the very idea of a written arrangement — that is the signal the rival predicts, and the response is not to press harder but to branch to truce-shaped arrangements (r8): owned zones, or rotations with a default outcome nobody must negotiate in the moment. Only if that branch also fails does the explicit what-is-this-flat conversation become next; by then it is warranted rather than front-loaded.

That sequencing is my main revision to the rival. R6 asks two people, one already avoiding chore conversations, to open with their theory of the household — a larger, more abstract ask than the conversations being avoided, and itself subject to the non-neutrality the rival charges against the account (r9's symmetric point: whichever reading you enact, the other side can experience it as an imposition). R7 extracts the same evidence from a smaller, concrete act.

What I reject: r3 used as a reason to abstain from proposing specifications at all. Non-neutrality is real but symmetrical — the rival's own interview also enacts a reading — so it prohibits everything or nothing; kept as a framing caution (small scope, explicitly revisable, individually delivered), it improves the move instead of forbidding it. I also reject, as premature, the idea that a reading must be settled before acting: the point of the merged move is that one need not choose.

What stays open: everything in the account's p1 (which chores, how long, whether the withdrawing friend has said why), plus what each flatmate actually wants the flat to be. Nothing yet decides whether the avoidance is conflict fatigue, principled preference, or load-dodging; r9 blocks the charitable assumption, the account's own limits block the uncharitable one, and the procedure works under all three.

Failure conditions, stated so they can happen: if even the two non-avoiding flatmates cannot agree three columns for two items between themselves, the ambiguity hypothesis fails at its easiest case and that path should be abandoned quickly; likewise if genuine content-engagement still leaves recurrence unchanged (u1's test). If the truce branch is refused wholesale, the convergent terminal move applies — the lease-and-fit question goes on the table by name. Practically, the reader is asked to run the next one to two weeks on two or three items and report both whether recurrence falls and how the proposals themselves were met. One housekeeping note: the rival's summary of the account matches the account I can read, though its citation (r1) points to an identifier not exposed here; the substance is checkable, so I treat it as sound while flagging the reference as unresolvable from this side.
